title: Ending a marriage without blame
subtitle: The no-fault regime under the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020
objectives: State the single ground for divorce and dissolution under the current law, and explain how it is established
Describe the statutory timeline from application to final order, including the 20-week reflection period and the minimum interval before a final order can be made
Apply the no-fault framework to a scenario, distinguishing sole from joint applications and identifying the narrow remaining bases on which an application can be disputed

leadingAuthorities.role: Replaced the fault-based five-facts system with a single no-fault ground, established by statement, for both divorce and civil partnership dissolution

leadingAuthorities.citation: Matrimonial Causes Act 1973, s 1 (as amended by the 2020 Act)
leadingAuthorities.role: The current statutory ground and procedure for divorce: irretrievable breakdown, established conclusively by a statement, leading to a divorce order

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often assume 'no-fault divorce' means there's nothing left to learn — no facts to memorise, no case law to apply. That's exactly backwards: the exam value in this topic is entirely procedural, in the timeline and the narrow grounds to contest. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the ground is irretrievable breakdown — this lesson checks whether you know the clock that runs after it's stated.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. Expect scenario questions built around dates and deadlines — when a conditional order can be sought, when a final order can follow.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be clear about what changed in 2022 before moving on — the rest of this lesson assumes you know there is now exactly one ground, established one way.

overview.hook: For nearly fifty years, ending a marriage in England and Wales usually meant proving something against your spouse — adultery, unreasonable behaviour, desertion — even where both of you simply wanted out. Since April 2022, none of that is true any more. A single statement that the marriage has broken down irretrievably is now, by itself, conclusive. The law didn't just simplify the paperwork; it deliberately removed blame from the legal process of ending a marriage, and replaced it with a clock.

parts.heading: The old law swept away
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Before 6 April 2022, a spouse seeking divorce had to prove the marriage had broken down irretrievably by establishing one of five specific facts: adultery, behaviour such that the petitioner could not reasonably be expected to live with the respondent, desertion for two years, two years' separation with the respondent's consent, or five years' separation without consent. In practice, most petitioners without two years to spare had to allege fault — adultery or behaviour — even in marriages that had ended amicably, because the 'no-fault' separation routes required a wait most people were not prepared to accept.

The system's weaknesses became impossible to ignore after Owens v Owens [2018] UKSC 41, in which a wife's petition based on her husband's behaviour was refused because the specific incidents she alleged were, in the court's assessment, not serious enough to meet the statutory test — leaving her legally married to a man she had left, unable to divorce him until five years' separation had run its course. The case did not change the law itself, but it crystallised long-standing criticism that requiring blame, in a marriage both parties agreed was over, served no one and often inflamed conflict that children and finances then had to be resolved around.

The Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 answered that criticism directly. It abolished the five facts entirely for applications made on or after 6 April 2022, replacing them with a single no-fault ground established by statement rather than by proof of conduct. The reform applies in parallel to civil partnership dissolution, amending the Civil Partnership Act 2004 in the same terms — everything in this lesson applies equally whether the relationship being ended is a marriage or a civil partnership, save for the change in vocabulary (divorce vs dissolution) already covered in Lesson 1.

components.definition: The system introduced by the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020, under which a party (or both parties jointly) need only state that the marriage has broken down irretrievably — with no requirement to prove adultery, behaviour, desertion or separation, and no ability for the other party to contest that statement on its merits.

interaction.prompt: Under the law as it stood before 6 April 2022, which of the following was NOT one of the five facts a petitioner could rely on to prove irretrievable breakdown?
options: Adultery
Two years' separation with consent
Unreasonable financial conduct
Behaviour such that the petitioner could not reasonably be expected to live with the respondent
interaction.trapExplanation: There was never a standalone 'unreasonable financial conduct' fact — financial conduct might have been folded into a behaviour-based petition, but the five facts were adultery, behaviour, desertion, two years' separation with consent, and five years' separation without consent.

parts.heading: The single ground: irretrievable breakdown by statement
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 1 of the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973, as substituted by the 2020 Act, now provides for exactly one ground: that the marriage has broken down irretrievably. What makes the new regime genuinely different from the old law is not the ground itself — 'irretrievable breakdown' was always the underlying legal test — but how it is established. Under the old five-facts system, irretrievable breakdown had to be proved by evidence of one of the facts. Under the current law, a statement by the applicant (or by both applicants, on a joint application) that the marriage has broken down irretrievably is, by itself, conclusive evidence of that breakdown.

'Conclusive' is doing real work in that sentence, and it is the detail examiners test most often: the court does not evaluate whether the statement is true, does not ask for supporting evidence, and cannot second-guess the applicant's assessment of their own marriage. Once a valid statement is made and the procedural requirements are met, the court must proceed on the basis that the marriage has broken down irretrievably — full stop.

This is a genuinely unusual legislative choice. In most areas of civil law, a bare assertion by one party is not conclusive of anything; here, Parliament deliberately removed the court's evaluative role because the alternative — litigating the state of a marriage's health — was judged to cause more harm than it prevented.

components.citation: Matrimonial Causes Act 1973, s 1 (as substituted by the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020)
components.text: (1) A marriage is dissolved by a divorce order made by the court... (2) An application for a divorce order may be made to the court by one or both parties to a marriage on the ground that the marriage has broken down irretrievably. (3) An application under subsection (2) must be accompanied by a statement by the applicant or applicants that the marriage has broken down irretrievably. (5) On an application under subsection (2), the court must— (a) take the statement... as conclusive evidence that the marriage has broken down irretrievably, and (b) make a divorce order.
elements: Application may be sole or joint
A statement of irretrievable breakdown must accompany the application, s 1(3)
The statement is conclusive evidence — the court cannot look behind it, s 1(5)(a)

interaction.prompt: Under s 1(5) MCA 1973 as amended, what must a court do once a valid statement of irretrievable breakdown has been made?
options: Treat the statement as conclusive evidence of breakdown and make a divorce order
Assess whether the marriage has genuinely broken down before proceeding
Require corroborating evidence from the other spouse
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The statement is expressly made conclusive — the court has no residual evaluative role once the procedural requirements are satisfied.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The statute removes the court's evaluative role entirely: once a valid statement is made, s 1(5)(a) requires the court to treat it as conclusive evidence of breakdown, not to test or corroborate it.

parts.heading: Sole and joint applications
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, working through a genuinely new feature
body: The 2020 Act introduced something the old law never allowed: a joint application, where both spouses apply together on the basis that the marriage has broken down irretrievably, rather than one spouse formally 'divorcing' the other. This was a deliberate attempt to reduce the adversarial framing of divorce proceedings even at the level of who is named as applicant and respondent.

A sole application still works broadly as before in structure — one spouse applies, and the other is the respondent — but without any fault to allege or defend against. If proceedings begin as a joint application and one applicant later no longer wishes to proceed jointly, the process allows the applicant who does wish to continue to switch to a sole application, so the process does not stall simply because the parties' cooperation breaks down partway through.

The choice between sole and joint application has no effect on the underlying test — both routes rest on exactly the same single ground, established the same way, and run to the same timeline. The distinction matters procedurally (who is named what, and what happens if one party stops cooperating) rather than substantively.

components.label: Sole vs joint applications
points: Sole application — one spouse applies; the other is the respondent, with no fault to allege or defend
Joint application — both spouses apply together, reflecting a shared, uncontested position that the marriage has broken down
A joint application can convert to a sole application if one party no longer wishes to proceed jointly
Both routes rest on the identical ground (irretrievable breakdown) and run the identical statutory timeline

interaction.prompt: Which scenario describes a joint application under the current law?
interaction.scenarioA: Mei and David both sign and submit the application together, each confirming the marriage has broken down irretrievably.
interaction.scenarioB: Mei applies alone; David receives the application as respondent and does not object to it.
interaction.explanation: A joint application requires both parties to apply together as applicants. B is a sole application — David not objecting doesn't change his status to co-applicant; he remains the respondent throughout.

parts.heading: The timeline: twenty weeks, then six weeks and a day
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: The 2020 Act did not remove all delay from the process — it replaced fault with time as the mechanism for ensuring divorce isn't rushed into. Two minimum periods matter, and examiners test the arithmetic precisely.

First, a minimum period of 20 weeks must run from the start of proceedings (when the application is issued) before the court can make a conditional order — the modern term for what used to be called decree nisi. This 20-week 'reflection period' is meant to give couples time to reflect on the decision and, where relevant, to begin addressing arrangements for children and finances, without holding up the process indefinitely.

Second, once a conditional order has been made, a further minimum period of six weeks and one day must pass before an application can be made for the final order — the modern term for decree absolute, and the point at which the marriage is actually dissolved. Adding the two periods together, the earliest a divorce can be finalised from the date proceedings begin is roughly 26 weeks — about six months — even where both parties agree from day one and nothing is contested.

The vocabulary change is worth fixing precisely, because older cases and some practitioner materials still use the pre-2022 terms: 'petition' is now 'application', 'decree nisi' is now 'conditional order', and 'decree absolute' is now 'final order'. An answer that uses the old terms is not wrong in substance, but using the current terms signals that you know the law as it stands today, not as it stood before the 2020 Act.

components.title: The statutory divorce timeline
components.description: The minimum periods that must elapse under the no-fault regime, from application to final order.

nodes.label: Application issued, with statement of irretrievable breakdown
Court may make a conditional order (formerly decree nisi)
Minimum further period of 6 weeks and 1 day must elapse
Application may be made for a final order (formerly decree absolute); marriage is dissolved

components.textAlternative: The process runs: application issued with a statement of irretrievable breakdown, then a minimum 20-week reflection period, after which the court may make a conditional order (formerly decree nisi), then a further minimum period of six weeks and one day, after which an application for a final order (formerly decree absolute) may be made, dissolving the marriage. The earliest realistic total is around 26 weeks.

interaction.prompt: Put these stages of the current divorce timeline in the correct order.
items: Application issued with statement of irretrievable breakdown
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the full sequence — and note the two separate minimum periods, one before the conditional order and a distinct, shorter one before the final order.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the two waiting periods again — the 20-week reflection period runs before the conditional order can be made; the shorter 6-week-and-1-day period runs between the conditional order and the final order, not before it.

parts.heading: Removal of the ability to contest
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: The clearest break with the old law is that a respondent can no longer contest a divorce application on its merits — a party cannot resist an application simply by disagreeing that the marriage has broken down, or by disputing the reasons behind the other party's statement. This is a deliberate and near-total change: under the old five-facts system, a respondent could in principle (as Owens illustrated) dispute the facts alleged; under the current law, the statement of irretrievable breakdown is conclusive, and there is nothing left on the merits to dispute.

A small number of narrow bases for disputing an application do survive, and they are jurisdictional or procedural rather than substantive: that the marriage was not validly formed in the first place (going back to Lesson 1's classification question, or Lesson 2's void grounds), that the court lacks jurisdiction to hear the case, that the proceedings were not validly issued or served, or that there has been fraud or, in rare cases, coercion vitiating the application itself. None of these routes allows a respondent to say, in substance, 'the marriage has not actually broken down' — that question has been taken out of the court's hands entirely.

This is the single most tested proposition in the topic, precisely because it feels counterintuitive: a legal process that used to be built around proving a marriage's failure is now built around a party simply saying so, with essentially no route for the other party to contradict that statement, however strongly they may disagree with it.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that a respondent 'can contest the divorce if they don't agree the marriage has broken down' — treating this as a live option analogous to defending a claim.
components.whyItsWrong: Since the statement of irretrievable breakdown is made conclusive by s 1(5) MCA 1973, disagreement about whether the marriage has genuinely broken down is not a basis for disputing the application at all. The only surviving bases are jurisdictional and procedural — validity of the marriage, jurisdiction, procedural compliance, or fraud/coercion vitiating the application — not disagreement with the substance of the statement.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a respondent can successfully dispute a divorce application purely on the basis that they do not believe the marriage has broken down?
sliderLabels: Confident — disagreement is a valid basis to dispute
Confident — disagreement is not a valid basis to dispute
interaction.correctPosition: disagreement is not a valid basis to dispute
interaction.explanation: Correct. The statement of irretrievable breakdown is conclusive under s 1(5). The only surviving bases to dispute an application are jurisdictional or procedural — such as the marriage's validity, the court's jurisdiction, or fraud or coercion — not simple disagreement with the applicant's assessment.

testPool.prompt: Name the single ground for divorce under the law as it currently stands.
testPool.modelAnswer: That the marriage has broken down irretrievably — established conclusively by a statement to that effect, under s 1 MCA 1973 as amended by the 2020 Act.

testPool.prompt: Name the modern statutory terms that replaced 'petition', 'decree nisi' and 'decree absolute'.
testPool.modelAnswer: Application (replacing petition), conditional order (replacing decree nisi), and final order (replacing decree absolute).

testPool.prompt: Did the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 remove the requirement to prove any of the five former facts (adultery, behaviour, desertion, and the two separation facts)?
options: Yes — none of the five facts need be proved; a statement of irretrievable breakdown is enough
No — the five facts still apply alongside the new statement requirement

testPool.prompt: Does the 2020 Act's no-fault regime apply to the dissolution of civil partnerships as well as to divorce?
options: Yes — the Act amends the Civil Partnership Act 2004 in parallel terms
No — civil partnership dissolution still requires proof of one of the old five facts

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that is legally irrelevant to whether the court must make a divorce order.
testPool.scenarioText: Priya applies for divorce, accompanying her application with a statement that the marriage has broken down irretrievably. Her husband Alex strongly disagrees, insisting the marriage can still be saved and that Priya is acting rashly after a single argument.
tappableSpans: accompanying her application with a statement
insisting the marriage can still be saved
testPool.correctSpan: insisting the marriage can still be saved
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Alex's belief that the marriage can be saved, however genuine, is legally irrelevant — the statement is conclusive under s 1(5), and disagreement about the marriage's true state is not a basis to dispute the application.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact the court is legally barred from considering. Alex's view that the marriage can still be saved goes to the merits of the statement — precisely what s 1(5) removes from the court's consideration.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would be a legitimate basis to dispute this application, unlike a simple disagreement about breakdown.
testPool.scenarioText: Tom receives a divorce application from someone claiming to be his wife. He has never been married to this person, and believes his signature on the underlying marriage documents was forged years ago by someone impersonating him.
tappableSpans: his signature on the underlying marriage documents was forged
testPool.correctSpan: his signature on the underlying marriage documents was forged
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. A challenge to the validity of the underlying marriage itself — here, potentially no valid marriage ever existed — is one of the narrow surviving bases to dispute proceedings, unlike disagreement about breakdown.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The legitimate basis here goes to whether a valid marriage exists at all, not to Tom's belief about who is applying. Look for the fact suggesting the marriage itself may never have been validly formed.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following remains a legitimate basis for a respondent to dispute a divorce application under the current law?
options: That the respondent does not believe the marriage has broken down
That the marriage was not validly formed in the first place
That the respondent would prefer a longer reflection period
That the applicant has behaved unreasonably during the marriage
testPool.trapExplanation: Disagreement with breakdown, a preference for more time, and allegations of unreasonable behaviour are all merits-based objections the 2020 Act deliberately removed. Disputing the underlying validity of the marriage is a genuinely surviving, jurisdictional basis — it goes to whether there was ever a marriage to dissolve.

testPool.prompt: Under s 1(3) MCA 1973 as amended, what must accompany a divorce application?
options: A statement that the marriage has broken down irretrievably
Evidence of at least one of the former five facts
A certificate from a marriage counsellor confirming reconciliation attempts
testPool.explanation: Section 1(3) requires the application to be accompanied by a statement of irretrievable breakdown — no evidence of a specific fact, and no counselling certificate, is required.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario correctly applies the minimum 20-week reflection period?
testPool.scenarioA: The application is issued on 1 January; the court makes a conditional order on 15 May of the same year, roughly 19 weeks later.
testPool.scenarioB: The application is issued on 1 January; the court makes a conditional order on 3 June of the same year, roughly 22 weeks later.
testPool.explanation: The conditional order cannot lawfully be made until a minimum of 20 weeks has elapsed from the application. Scenario A falls short of that minimum; scenario B satisfies it.

testPool.prompt: Order these historical and legal developments correctly.
items: The five-facts system requires proof of adultery, behaviour, desertion or separation to establish irretrievable breakdown
Owens v Owens highlights the difficulty of a contested behaviour-based petition
The Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 is enacted
The no-fault regime, including the statement of irretrievable breakdown, comes into force on 6 April 2022

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a divorce can lawfully be finalised in less than 20 weeks from the date the application is issued, even where both parties fully agree from the outset?
sliderLabels: Confident — it can be finalised sooner
Confident — it cannot be finalised sooner
testPool.explanation: The 20-week reflection period is a statutory minimum before the conditional order, and a further 6 weeks and 1 day is required before the final order — neither period can be shortened by agreement, however cooperative both parties are.

testPool.prompt: Sam and Jordan submit a joint application for divorce, each confirming in the statement that their marriage has broken down irretrievably. Three months later, Jordan changes their mind and no longer wishes the divorce to proceed on the ground that the marriage has, in fact, not broken down. Analyse whether Jordan can prevent the divorce continuing.
factsToOrder: Sam and Jordan submit a joint application with a statement of irretrievable breakdown
Jordan changes their mind and now believes the marriage has not broken down
Jordan wishes to prevent the divorce continuing on that basis

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Jordan can prevent the divorce continuing on the basis that they no longer believe the marriage has broken down.
modelAnswer.rule: Under s 1(5) MCA 1973 as amended, a statement of irretrievable breakdown is conclusive evidence of breakdown; a party cannot dispute an application on the substantive ground that the marriage has not broken down. Where a joint application is made and one applicant no longer wishes to proceed jointly, the process allows the other applicant to continue as a sole applicant rather than requiring the whole application to fail.
modelAnswer.application: Jordan's change of heart, however sincere, is precisely the kind of substantive objection s 1(5) forecloses — a party cannot withdraw the conclusive effect of a statement already made by simply disagreeing with it later. What Jordan can do is decline to continue as a joint applicant, but that converts the application to a sole one at Sam's instigation rather than stopping the divorce outright.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Jordan cannot prevent the divorce continuing on the ground that the marriage has not broken down; at most, Jordan's withdrawal converts the application from joint to sole, with Sam able to continue it alone.

testPool.prompt: An applicant issues a divorce application on 1 March. Assuming no delays, what is the earliest date on which the court could make a conditional order?
options: Roughly mid-July, once the 20-week minimum has elapsed
1 April, one month later
There is no minimum period before a conditional order
testPool.explanation: The 20-week reflection period runs from the date the application is issued, so the earliest a conditional order can be made is roughly 20 weeks after 1 March — around mid-July, not sooner.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that most precisely explains why the statement of irretrievable breakdown removes the court's evaluative role.
testPool.passage: Under the old five-facts system, irretrievable breakdown had to be proved by evidence of a specific fact, and a court could in principle assess whether that evidence met the statutory test. Under the current law, s 1(5) requires the court to take a statement of irretrievable breakdown as conclusive evidence of that breakdown, so the court's role shifts from evaluating evidence to confirming that the procedural requirements for a valid statement have been met.
testPool.ratioSentence: Under the current law, s 1(5) requires the court to take a statement of irretrievable breakdown as conclusive evidence of that breakdown, so the court's role shifts from evaluating evidence to confirming that the procedural requirements for a valid statement have been met.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is assuming a respondent can still contest a divorce by disagreeing that the marriage has broken down. Since the statement of irretrievable breakdown is made conclusive by s 1(5) MCA 1973, the only surviving bases to dispute an application are jurisdictional or procedural — never a disagreement with the substance of the statement itself.
